stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点: CloudflareがDenoを買収し、1年間のバグフィックスとセキュリティアップデートを含む月次リリースでサポートを継続した後、開発を終了すると発表したこと。コミュニティでは、Denoの当初のシンプルさとセキュリティ第一の設計がnpm互換性へのシフトで失われ、バローンが膨らんだことが指摘され、さらに買収により他企業がDenoを引き継いでcelldなどのエッジランタイム基盤を育てる可能性が閉ざされる懸念も示された。  
賛否両論: 賛成派は、Cloudflare WorkersのエッジランタイムにDenoを組み込むことで、セルフホスト可能なセルD（celld）の基盤強化や、Workerdとの統合による完全なバックエンドインボックス実現への期待を示す。否定派は、初期のDenoが持っていた「Node.jsを最初から作り直す」理想がVCプレッシャーで放棄され、オープンソースとしての将来が不透明になったことに悲しみを表明し、Node.jsがDenoの良い機能を取り入れたことは救いだが十分ではないと嘆く。  
注目コメント: 一ユーザーは「早期のDenoはNode.jsを改善させた遺産がある」と指摘し、もう一人は「買収の見出しは『CloudflareによるDenoの実質的な開発終了』が適切」とツッコミ、さらにセルDとWorkerdの違いに関心を持ち、セルフホストの完全バックエンドへの可能性に期待を寄せたコメントが注目された。
stories.editor_note: CloudflareがDenoを買収したことは、エッジとサーバーレスの境界を曖昧にし、国内のクラウドネイティブ開発者が関数ベースのアーキテクチャを世界規模で試せる環境を整える点で注目されており、特に日本のIoTスタートアップにとって低遅延デプロイのハードルが下がる期待がある。

comments.author: acgourley
comments.text: Very cool. I'm working on a similar project for contemporary political opinion media. Every podcast, blog, oped, or show cut into little pieces with the structure, speaker, quotes and nouns pulled out and cross-referenced. I bring it up because I wonder if this kind of heavy-weight preprocessing is worth bringing to historical documents as well. It would be much more expensive, initially, but afterwards allows questions get answered even cheaper than they are in your current system. It may be worth collecting interested parties and co-investing in the structured parsing. Also modern transcription and historical document scanning have a similar shaped problem - dealing with misspelled words and trying to infer their corrections from context.

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点  
ビジュアルエフェクト（回転するサイ隕石アニメーションなど）の必要性と、研究ワークフローをオープンソースしたツールキット Antiquity の紹介、さらに過去のアーカイブへの重処理前処理の価値について議論された。

・賛否両論  
エフェクトについては「邪魔で satirical」という批判と、「記事上部にオフにできるオプションがあるので問題ない」という擁護が対立。ツールキットへの肯定的反応は共通だが、重処理前処理については「初期コストは高いが後続のクエリが安くなる」という賛成と、「現状の方法で十分」という慎重意見に分かれた。

・注目コメント  
1. 「記事の最上部にエフェクトをオフにするスイッチがある」と指摘し、論争を実用的に回避できる点を挙げたコメント。  
2. 「政治メディア向けの同様のプロジェクトを進めており、過去文書にも同じ前処理が有望だが初期投資が必要」と、 transcription・スキャンの課題と結びつけて洞察を示したコメント。
stories.editor_note: 400年分の古文書アーカイブにAIを適用した事例は、日本の地方自治体が進めるデジタルアーカイブプロジェクトにおいて、文字認識と地学知識を組み合わせることで忘れられた文化遺産や自然現象の再発見を促す可能性を示しており、学際的研究の新たなモデルとして注目されている。

**注目コメント**：あるユーザーは「JeVリリース後すぐに多数の意思決定モデルが登場し、OpenAIのAPIがそれを上回る」と述べ、別のユーザーは「VCが技術レベルでのデューデリジェンスを徹底しているはずなのに、この評価は理解できない」と投稿し、ハイクサイクルのピークを疑問視している。
stories.editor_note: Typesafe AIの870Mドル調達は、AIインフラ分野への投資熱が再燃していることを示し、日本のAIスタートアップも同様の大規模資金調達を狙う動きが活発になり、国内VCも海外並みのメガラウンドを検討し始めている背景がある。

comments.author: herbertl
comments.text: While I like the punchy title, I'd suggest the often invisible role of preliminary work IS a part of being creative. In music it's "demos," in art it's "sketches," in writing it's "drafts," etc. I write in my book, Creative Doing: > This stage is far too early to demand perfection; it’s best to keep expectations low, to refrain from self-criticism, and to support psychological safety (the feeling that it’s okay to make mistakes) to allow every single detail of the idea to flow out. It's related to the original post's mention of scarcity, and how "the path to writing a great song really is through hundreds of mediocre songs." The most reliable way to good work is to allow it to emerge through a lot of preliminary work (e.g., lots of drafts, demos, and sketches). More on preliminary work here: https://www.holloway.com/g/creative-doing/sections/draft-dem...

comments.text: I'm paying for the heavily-discounted subscriptions, not the API rates. There isn't really a cost gap for me. DeepSeek doesn't have a subscription to compare to, but when I compared the GLM 5.3 usage I got from a $100/mo Z.ai subscription compared to Opus 5.5 on a $100/mo Claude subscription, there wasn't a big gap. And GLM 5.3 is very clearly not a frontier model (deepseek v4 seemed a lot closer, but I didn't use it enough to really say for my workloads). I don't think those subscriptions nave negative contribution margins, either. I think we're seeing a lot of price discrimination by the big labs, and huge margins on their frontier models. The fact that they have been cutting prices to their second-biggest tier of models (Opus/Sol). Open models catching up and collapsing these margins would worry me if I were a shareholder in the big labs, but as a user, I really doubt that the western labs have bigger environmental impact just because they have higher API costs, I think they have a ton of efficiencies they aren't sharing with customers yet because demand is so high.

comments.text: Marketing. Have you guys see how aggressive is the push for enterprise use by both OpenAI and Anthropic? I had friend from a non-tech industry in Asia telling me that their company was offered free trial of the enterprise version of Claude, with trainings and such. On the other hand, DS and Z.ai, have zero to none marketing outside China. There is friction to use DS/GlM models and the ZDR is unclear, so most enterprise that has heavy AI usage hasn't move over yet. They would rather spent $200 for the peace of mind than to take the risk of being slam as a national traitor down the road (which again is another form of marketing by Big AI, trying to frame Chinese models as thiefs). So, I don't think they are not freaking out, it's just that they are addressing different market segments and reacting to the situation differently.

DeepSeek is horrible at grilling sessions (the /grill* skills to make technical decisions). It doesn't know how to explain things. Maybe the skill could be adjusted. It also doesn't come up with as good solutions as Opus/Sol. What I use it for is * the orchestator of my coding workflows * the tester/verifier of code changes * the sub agent that explores code or does web searches * putting together code base research reports Previously I planned with Opus/Sol/Astra and then I used DeepSeek for coding, and then reviewed with Opus/Sol/Astra. With the cost improvements to Opus/Sol I am trying to use them for coding instead now so there will be less back and forth review needed. They are all working together in Pi using the extension @tintinweb/pi-subagents where my workflow skill is calling different subagents that use different models. Luna is cost competitive, but doesn't score as well on intelligence. I do need the intelligence for most of what I use it for, so I am not motivated to use Luna. Haiku also doesn't seem like a competitive price/performance mix.

It now doesn't dial to Amazon at all - it does all processing locally with its own CPU and connects to my homeassistant for home automation. My initial setup involved qwen asr (1.7b model) running on rtx 5080. Compared to that, whistle was really bad (out of 170 messages, qwen recognized correctly 168, whistle - 70), but I adjusted whistle to work like jev - instead of free form transcription it recognizes only select set of templates (I trained tiny network with 10,000 generated utterances to translate whistle final state to probabilities within templates). comments.author: schopra909
comments.text: Hi HN, author here! For context, we're a 2-person lab training generative video models. Goal is a new set of controllable, animation tools (you can read more about that here https://www.linum.ai/about if you're curious). The biggest bottleneck for our last text-to-video model in terms of training and inference cost is attention. Video models are incredibly token dense (e.g. 110K tokens for a several second clip). If we can condense that context window more aggressively, we can train bigger models for a lot less $$ and offer them to prosumers at reasonable price points (unlike the big models today like Seedance, which cost an arm and a leg to run). Traditionally, image and video models have two disjoint components: VAE (Variational Autoencoder) and Diffusion Transformer (DiT). They're trained separately, and empirically VAEs seems to struggle to get past 16x16 token reduction. Here, we're switching to pixel-space, throwing away the VAE, and achieving 32x32 token reduction (4x smaller context windows) while learning a better overall model in a fraction of the training samples. The central thesis is "simpler is better". If we can put the compression problem into the more powerful Diffusion Transformer (DiT) would should be able to learn a "latent space" optimized for generation and get better compression without hurting generation quality. I'll be checking this post off and on the next couple of hours, so feel free to drop questions below. And I'll try to answer them to the best of my ability. P.S. The model checkpoints from this blog are Apache 2.0, so feel to try playing with it yourself on a GPU!

comments.author: layer8
comments.text: > Is Coding → Prompting like Assembly → High Level Coding? […] I do not agree with this simile. Compilers are, for the most part, deterministic in a way that current AI tools are not. It’s not quite about the determinism. It’s about being able to reason about the relationship between source code and compiled program with formal precision. You can predict which changes in the source code will lead to which exact changes in the behavior of the compiled program. The same isn’t the case about changes to an LLM prompt and the LLM’s output. You could make an AI deterministic by fixing its source of randomness. That still wouldn’t allow you to reason about how its output will change when (for example) you add or remove a word in the prompt. The only way to find out is to run the LLM (= have the prompt run through the model and observe what comes out). That is the fundamental difference. Changes to source code have predictable and reason-able outcomes. You generally don’t have to compile the code and test it to know how precisely the change will affect the behavior of the compiled program according to the semantics of the programming language. That’s the case even if the compiler uses some probabilistic heuristics for trade-offs in code generation, and hence isn’t deterministic on the machine code level. To repeat, the difference is how you can reason about a compiler’s behavior versus an LLM’s behavior. Programming languages are designed such that you can reason about it. With LLMs it’s always an experiment.

I've found that I have to teach them and also document a lot of basic computer idioms -- Control-C / X / A / V to copy, cut, select all, paste; but also more basic things, like the fact there are two pointers on the screen -- one for the mouse and one for the keyboard -- if you slide the mouse pointer to a specific point and press a keyboard key, the new key will not appear where the arrow is, it will appear where the text cursor is. A big one was tabs. I had to get a couple of manilla folders and show them the actual tabs, and hold it up next to the browser with several tabs, and suddenly it snapped with them what the interface was trying to represent. Control-A will select all of a web page, unless you are in the text entry box of a form, then it selects just the things in that text entry box. I started writing this up in a little manual, it got to a dozen pages fast, and I haven't put very much in it. comments.text: These kinds of tools are very useful. I have my own called memo (which is just a shell script: https://github.com/aktau/dotfiles/blob/master/bin/memo ). It was discussed in https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45670052 and others chimed in with their own (like bkt(1) and up(1)). The main differences I see: - memo doesn't need to be built (its a shell script) - once keeps output cache in a running daemon. By contrast, memo stores content under /tmp with whatever the best compression available is (it prefers zstd). There's trade-offs in that. More pareto-optimal from the security front may be to have a sort of session key and to compress-then-encrypt files on disk.

stories.summary_ja: 「once」というツールは、CLIコマンドの出力をキャッシュして再実行を省く仕組みで、特に1Passwordのcredential取得のように秘密情報を毎回求められる場面で有用だという意見が多かった。一方で、キャッシュをディスクに残すことによるセキュリティリスクや、デーモン起動が必要な点、コマンドにプレフィックスを付ける手間が議論になった。自分はシェルスクリプトのmemoを使っており、ビルド不要かつ/tmpに圧縮保存（zstd優先）する点が利点だが、デーモン方式のonceは常駐キャッシュにより高速になる反面、セッションキーと暗号化を組み合わせた方が安全だと指摘された。さらに、OSが出力のメタデータから再実行の必要性を判断できる仕組み（NixOSのビルドキャッシュのように）を一般プロセスにも適用したいという願望や、onceプレフィックスを不要にしてスクロールバックから直接grepできるような「output」コンセプトへの期待が示された。
stories.editor_note: OnceによるCLIコマンドキャッシュは、シェルスクリプトや自動化パイプラインでの同じコマンドの再実行を減らし、日本のDevOpsエンジニアがターミナル作業の効率向上とコスト削減を両立させるために活用が広がっており、特にCI/CDパイプラインでの冗長ステップ削減に有効である背景がある。

stories.summary_ja: コメントではまず記事中のタイポが指摘され、著者が「callback」「errback」などの説明的名前を美観のために「deferred」「promise」へ変更したことを批判し、名前が機能を表さなくなったと指摘している。次に、型レベル計算によるバグ防止やコードの短縮、Haskell学習時の感動や富士山の景色との類比から、プログラミングにも芸術と同様の美的体験があり、訓練がなければ理解しづらいと主張している。さらに、Einsteinの「純粋数学は論理的アイデアの詩」を引き、プログラミングと数学は一般人には異質な芸術形式であり、人間が「これは私の作ったもの」と宣言する意図的行為が芸術性の核だと議論されている。賛否については、名前変更の美観重視に疑問を呈する声と、抽象化による表現力向上を支持する声が分かれている。また、一部のコメントでは、名前の変更が抽象化を進め、複雑な非同期フローを扱いやすくしたと評価する一方で、当初の名前が挙動を直感的に示していたため、初学者へのハードルが下がっていたと指摘している。さらに、プログラミングを芸術と見なす立場では、コードを読む行為が美術館の解説文を読むことに例えられ、理解のための努力が美的満足を深めるという観点が示されている。一方で、実用性を重視する声は、プログラミングは問題解決のための道具であり、芸術として鑑賞するよりも機能性が優先されるべきだと主張している。最後に、オープンソースコミュニティにおける共同制作が、多数の人間が「これは私の作ったもの」と言える場を提供し、これが集合的な芸術形成であると見なす意見も見られた。
stories.editor_note: プログラミングが特別なスキルではなく問題解決の思考法であるという認識は、日本の教育現場では論理的思考を育むカリキュラムが重視され、単なるコード記述よりもアルゴリズム設計能力の育成が重要視されている背景がある。

comments.text: I use a Raspberry Pi, not a VPS -- as others state, Codex/Claude Code alongside things like Cloudflare and Tailscale make self hosting far easier. People have commented a lot already, but one thing I do that I haven't seen others already doing yet is I run a news summarization pipeline with Miniflux and Flatnotes. All my feeds are in one of two categories; Summarize and NoSummarize. Once a day, a script fires at everything unread in the Summarize category, pulls the full text from Miniflux (or calls a scraping service if it appears to only have an article stub), groups similar articles to together with a 60 to 80 word summary, and for everything not grouped together it gives each article a 20 word or so summary. Just enough for me to know if it warrants a full read or not. Then it takes that a posts the digest to a markdown file in a Flatnotes folder. Flatnotes I expose via Tailscale Funnel so I can read it anywhere, including on my work laptop if I'm at the office. Why Miniflux and Flatnotes and not other options? Mostly because those two are about as lightweight as it gets with still pleasing interfaces and basic features.

comments.text: By my standards (lowendspirit.com) $5/month is kind of high end for a VPS. I have a small personal web site on a $4 per year VPS. Other than that I have another VPS (I think around $7/m with 500GB of HDD) that I use as a personal storage server and git repo since its internet connection is much faster than my home one, etc. For a while I ran some monitoring tasks on VPSes, though I don't have any active right now. tierhive.com has super cheap VPS, as low as 10 cents/month for a tiny one (128MB ram, 1GB SSD). ipv6 only, with a NAT proxy for ipv4 I think. It's quite possible to run a useful basic Debian server on that. I ran one with 32MB ram for a while.

stories.summary_ja: コミュニティでは、5ドル/月のVPSで常時稼働させる価値のあるサービスとして、メディアサーバー（qBittorrent＋Jellyfin、Immich、Tailscaleで外部アクセス）、自己ホスト型Git（Gitea）、個人用クラウドストレージ・フォトアルバム、自動化ダッシュボードやTodoリスト、ニュース要約パイプライン（Miniflux＋Flatnotes＋Tailscale Funnel）、軽量監視やバックアップ、Oracle Always FreeでのMinecraftサーバーなどが挙げられた。賛否は、5ドルはむしろ高めであり、さらに安いプロバイダーやRaspberry Pi＋Tailscale構成でも十分だと指摘する声と、リソース制約があるため軽量かつ特定用途に絞った運用が必須だという意見に分かれた。特に注目されたのは、毎日起動するニュース要約スクリプトで、未読記事を要約しFlatnotesに出力し、Tailscaleでどこからでも閲覧できる仕組みを紹介したコメントで、自動化とプライベート情報へのアクセスの両立例として高く評価された。
